title: VI. A Laceration In The Cottage
paragraphs: He was truly distressed, as he seldom had been before. He had rushed in like a fool, and meddled in what? A love affair. “But what do I know about it? What can I tell about such things?” he said to himself for the hundredth time, flushing crimson. “Oh, feeling ashamed would be nothing; shame is only the punishment I deserve. The trouble is that I’ve surely caused more unhappiness.... And Father Zossima sent me to reconcile them and bring them together. Is this how you bring them together?” Then he suddenly remembered how he had tried to join their hands, and felt dreadfully ashamed all over again. “I acted quite sincerely, but I’ll have to be more sensible from now on,” he concluded suddenly, and he didn’t even smile at his own conclusion.

Katerina Ivanovna’s errand took him to Lake Street, and his brother Dmitri lived close by, in a side street off it. Alyosha decided to go to Dmitri in any case before seeing the captain, though he felt sure he wouldn’t find him. He suspected that Dmitri would purposely avoid him now, but he had to find him anyhow. Time was passing. Ever since he left the monastery, the thought of his dying elder had not left him for a single minute.

One thing about Katerina Ivanovna’s errand interested him especially. When she spoke of the captain’s son, the little schoolboy who had run beside his father crying, Alyosha had at once been struck by the idea that this must be the schoolboy who had bitten his finger when he, Alyosha, asked what he had done to hurt him. Now Alyosha felt almost sure of it, though he couldn’t have said why. Turning his mind to something else was a relief, and he resolved to stop dwelling on the “mischief” he had done and not to torture himself with remorse, but to do what he had to do, whatever came of it. That thought comforted him completely. Turning into the street where Dmitri lodged, he felt hungry, so he took the roll he had brought from his father’s out of his pocket and ate it. It made him feel stronger.

Dmitri was not at home. The people of the house, an old cabinet-maker, his son and his old wife, eyed Alyosha with downright suspicion. “He hasn’t slept here these last three nights. He may have gone away,” the old man said, in answer to Alyosha’s repeated questions. Alyosha could tell that he was answering on orders. When he asked whether Dmitri might be at Grushenka’s, or hiding at Foma’s (Alyosha spoke so openly on purpose), all three looked at him in alarm. “They’re fond of him, they’re doing their best for him,” thought Alyosha. “That’s good.”

At last he found the house in Lake Street. It was a rickety little house, sagging on one side, with three windows facing the street and a muddy yard, where a lone cow stood in the middle. He crossed the yard and found the door that led into the passage. To the left of the passage lived the old woman of the house and her old daughter. Both seemed to be deaf. He asked for the captain over and over, until one of them finally grasped that he wanted their lodgers, and pointed to a door across the passage. The captain’s lodging turned out to be a plain peasant’s room. Alyosha had his hand on the iron latch when the strange silence inside struck him. Yet he knew from Katerina Ivanovna’s words that the man had a family. “Either they’re all asleep, or maybe they heard me coming and are waiting for me to open the door. I’d better knock first,” he thought, and knocked. An answer came, but not right away, after a gap of perhaps ten seconds.
“Who is it?” somebody shouted, in a loud and very angry voice.

Then Alyosha opened the door and stepped over the threshold. He found himself in a regular peasant’s room. It was large, but it was crammed with household belongings of every kind, and there were several people in it. On the left stood a big Russian stove. A string ran from the stove across the room to the window on the left, with rags hanging on it. Against the wall on each side, right and left, stood a bedstead covered with knitted quilts. On the left-hand one was a pyramid of four print-covered pillows, each smaller than the one below it. On the other there was just one very small pillow. The corner opposite was screened off by a curtain, or a sheet hung on a string. Behind the curtain you could see a bed made up on a bench, and a chair. The rough square table of plain wood had been pushed up to the middle window. The three windows, each made of four tiny greenish, mildewed panes, gave little light and were shut tight, so the room was rather dark and stuffy. On the table stood a frying pan with the remains of some fried eggs, a half-eaten piece of bread, and a small bottle with a few drops of vodka.

A genteel-looking woman in a cotton gown sat on a chair by the bed on the left. Her face was thin and yellow, and her sunken cheeks told you at first glance that she was ill. But what struck Alyosha most was the look in the poor woman’s eyes—a look of surprised inquiry and yet of haughty pride. And all the while he was talking to her husband, her big brown eyes moved from one speaker to the other with the same haughty, questioning look. Beside her at the window stood a young girl, rather plain, with thin reddish hair, poorly but very neatly dressed. She gave Alyosha a disdainful look as he came in. By the other bed sat another female figure. She was a very sad sight, a girl of about twenty, hunchbacked and crippled, “with withered legs,” as Alyosha was told afterwards. Her crutches stood in the corner close by. This poor girl’s strikingly beautiful, gentle eyes rested on Alyosha with mild serenity. At the table sat a man of forty-five, finishing the fried eggs. He was lean, small and weakly built. He had reddish hair and a thin, light-colored beard, very like a wisp of tow (this comparison and the phrase “a wisp of tow” flashed into Alyosha’s mind at once, for some reason, and he remembered it afterwards). Clearly this was the gentleman who had shouted, since there was no other man in the room. But when Alyosha came in, he jumped up from the bench he was sitting on and, hastily wiping his mouth with a ragged napkin, darted over to Alyosha.
“It’s a monk come begging for the monastery. A fine place to come to!” said the girl standing in the left corner, loudly. The man spun round to her at once and answered in an excited, cracking voice:
“No, Varvara, you’re mistaken. Allow me to ask,” he turned to Alyosha again, “what brings you to—our retreat?”

Alyosha studied him closely. It was the first time he had seen him. There was something angular, flustered and touchy about him. He had clearly been drinking, but he was not drunk. His look was extraordinarily impudent, and yet, strange to say, frightened at the same time. He looked like a man who had been kept down for a long time and had put up with it, and who had now suddenly turned and was trying to stand up for himself. Or, better still, like a man who badly wants to hit you but is terribly afraid you’ll hit him. His words and the tone of his shrill voice had a kind of crazy humor, now spiteful and now cringing, and always shifting from one note to the other. He had asked his question about “our retreat” trembling all over, rolling his eyes, and hopping up so close to Alyosha that Alyosha instinctively stepped back. He wore a very shabby dark cotton coat, patched and stained. His checked trousers were of an extremely pale color, long out of fashion, and made of very thin cloth. They were so crumpled and so short that he looked like a boy who had outgrown them.
“I’m Alexey Karamazov,” Alyosha began, in reply.
“I know that perfectly well, sir,” the gentleman snapped out at once, to make clear that he already knew who he was. “I am Captain Snegiryov, sir, but I still want to know exactly what has led you—”
“Oh, I’ve come about nothing in particular. I wanted a word with you—if you’ll let me.”

“In that case, here’s a chair, sir; kindly be seated. That’s what they used to say in the old comedies, ‘kindly be seated,’” and with a quick motion he grabbed an empty chair (a rough wooden one, not upholstered) and put it for him almost in the middle of the room. Then he took another just like it for himself and sat down facing Alyosha, so close that their knees nearly touched.

“Nikolay Ilyitch Snegiryov, sir, formerly a captain in the Russian infantry, disgraced by his vices, but still a captain. Though I may not be one anymore, going by the way I talk. For the second half of my life I’ve been learning to say ‘sir.’ It’s a word you use once you’ve come down in the world.”
“That’s very true,” smiled Alyosha. “But does it slip out on its own, or do you use it on purpose?”

“As God’s my witness, it just comes out! I never used to say it. All my life I said ‘sir’ to nobody. Then the moment I sank into low water, I started saying ‘sir.’ Some higher power did that. I can see you’re interested in the questions of the day. But how could I possibly have roused your curiosity, living as I do where there’s no room for hospitality at all?”
“I’ve come—about that business.”
“What business?” the captain cut in impatiently.
“About what happened between you and my brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Alyosha blurted out clumsily.

“What happened, sir? Surely not that? Is it my ‘wisp of tow’ you mean?” He leaned in so close that his knees actually knocked against Alyosha’s. His lips were pressed into a strange, thin line, like a thread.
“What wisp of tow?” Alyosha muttered.

“He’s come to complain about me, Father!” cried a voice Alyosha knew, the schoolboy’s, from behind the curtain. “I bit his finger just now.” The curtain was pulled back, and Alyosha saw the boy who had attacked him, lying on a little bed made up from the bench and a chair in the corner under the ikons. He lay under his coat and an old quilted blanket. He was clearly ill, and from the glitter in his eyes he had a fever. He looked at Alyosha without any fear, as if he knew he was at home and nobody could touch him.
“What! He bit your finger?” The captain leaped from his chair. “It was your finger he bit?”

“Yes. He was throwing stones with some other schoolboys, six of them against him alone. I walked up to him, and he threw a stone at me, then another one at my head. I asked him what I’d ever done to him. Then he rushed me and bit my finger badly. I don’t know why.”
“I’ll thrash him, sir, this very minute!” The captain sprang up again.
“But I’m not complaining at all, I’m only telling you ... I don’t want him thrashed. Besides, he looks ill.”

“And you think I’d thrash him? That I’d take my Ilusha and thrash him right in front of you, to give you satisfaction? Would you like it done now, sir?” said the captain, suddenly rounding on Alyosha as if he meant to fly at him. “I’m sorry about your finger, sir. But instead of thrashing Ilusha, would you rather I chopped off my own four fingers with this knife, here, before your eyes, to satisfy your just anger? Four fingers, I’d think, should be enough to slake your thirst for revenge. You won’t be asking for the fifth as well?” He broke off, his voice catching in his throat. Every feature of his face was twitching and working, and he looked wildly defiant. He was in a kind of frenzy.

“I think I see it all now,” said Alyosha, gently and sadly, still sitting where he was. “So your boy is a good boy. He loves his father, and he went for me because I’m the brother of the man who wronged you.... Now I see,” he repeated thoughtfully. “My brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch is sorry for what he did, I know that. If he can possibly come to you—or better still, meet you at the very same place—he’ll ask your forgiveness in front of everyone, if you want him to.”
“After he’s pulled out my beard, you mean, he’ll ask my forgiveness? And he thinks that will wrap it up nicely, does he?”
“Oh, no! Quite the opposite. He’ll do whatever you like, and however you like.”
“So if I were to ask his highness to go down on his knees before me in that very tavern—‘The Metropolis,’ it’s called—or in the marketplace, he’d do it?”
“Yes, he would even go down on his knees.”

“You’ve pierced me to the heart, sir. You’ve brought me to tears, and pierced me to the heart! I’m only too well aware of your brother’s generosity. Let me introduce my family: my two daughters and my son—my litter. If I die, who’ll look after them? And as long as I live, who but them will care about a wretch like me? That’s a great thing the Lord has arranged for every man of my sort, sir. Because there has to be someone who can love even a man like me.”
“Ah, that’s perfectly true!” exclaimed Alyosha.
“Oh, stop playing the fool! Some idiot walks in, and you put us to shame!” cried the girl by the window, suddenly turning to her father with a scornful, contemptuous look.
“Wait a bit, Varvara!” her father cried sharply, though he looked at her quite approvingly. “That’s her character,” he told Alyosha again.
“And in all nature there was naught That could find favor in his eyes—

or rather, to put it in the feminine, that could find favor in her eyes. But now let me present you to my wife, Arina Petrovna. She’s a cripple, forty-three years old; she can move, but only a very little. She comes of humble people. Arina Petrovna, compose your face. This is Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov. Get up, Alexey Fyodorovitch.” He took him by the hand and, with surprising strength, hauled him to his feet. “You have to stand to be introduced to a lady. This isn’t the Karamazov, mamma, who ... h’m ... et cetera, but his brother, radiant with modest virtues. Come now, Arina Petrovna, come, mamma, first, your hand to be kissed.”

And he kissed his wife’s hand with respect, even tenderness. The girl at the window turned her back on it all in disgust. Over the proud, questioning face of the woman came a look of extraordinary warmth.
“Good morning! Sit down, Mr. Tchernomazov,” she said.
“Karamazov, mamma, Karamazov. We come of humble people,” he whispered again.

“Well, Karamazov, or whatever it is, I always think of Tchernomazov.... Sit down. Why did he haul you up? He calls me a cripple, but I’m not. It’s just that my legs are swollen like barrels, and the rest of me has shriveled up. I used to be so fat, and now it’s as if I’d swallowed a needle.”
“We come of humble people,” the captain muttered again.
“Oh, Father, Father!” said the hunchback girl, who until then had sat silent on her chair, and she hid her eyes in her handkerchief.
“Buffoon!” the girl at the window burst out.

“Have you heard our news?” said the mother, pointing at her daughters. “It’s like clouds rolling in; the clouds pass and we have music again. When we were with the army, we had plenty of guests like this. I’m not comparing anyone, mind; each to their own taste. The deacon’s wife used to come then and say, ‘Alexandr Alexandrovitch is a man with the noblest heart, but Nastasya Petrovna,’ she’d say, ‘is a child of hell.’ ‘Well,’ I said, ‘that’s a matter of taste, but you’re a little spitfire.’ ‘And you need putting in your place,’ says she. ‘You black sword,’ said I, ‘who asked you to teach me?’ ‘But my breath,’ says she, ‘is clean, and yours is foul.’ ‘Go and ask all the officers if my breath is foul.’ And I’ve had it on my mind ever since. Just the other day I was sitting here, just as I am now, when I saw that same general walk in, the one who came here at Easter, and I asked him: ‘Your Excellency,’ said I, ‘can a lady’s breath be unpleasant?’ ‘Yes,’ he answered; ‘you ought to open a window-pane or the door, because the air in here isn’t fresh.’ That’s how they all carry on! And what is my breath to them? The dead smell worse! ‘I won’t spoil the air,’ said I, ‘I’ll order some slippers and be off.’ My darlings, don’t blame your own mother! Nikolay Ilyitch, why can’t I please you? Only Ilusha comes home from school and loves me. Yesterday he brought me an apple. Forgive your own mother—forgive a poor lonely creature! Why has my breath become so unpleasant to you?”
And the poor mad woman broke down in sobs, with tears running down her cheeks. The captain ran over to her.

“Mamma, mamma, my dear, don’t, don’t! You’re not lonely. Everyone loves you, everyone adores you.” He began kissing both her hands again and tenderly stroking her face. Then he took the dinner napkin and started wiping away her tears. Alyosha thought there were tears in his eyes too. “There, you see? You hear?” he said, wheeling on Alyosha in a sort of fury and pointing at the poor imbecile.
“I see and I hear,” muttered Alyosha.
“Father, Father, how can you—with him! Leave him be!” cried the boy, sitting up in bed and staring at his father with blazing eyes.
“Enough of this clowning! Enough of your silly antics that never come to anything!” shouted Varvara, stamping her foot in a passion.

“This time your anger is perfectly just, Varvara, and I’ll hurry to satisfy you. Come, Alexey Fyodorovitch, put on your cap, and I’ll put on mine. We’ll go out. I have something serious to say to you, but not inside these walls. This girl sitting here is my daughter Nina. I forgot to introduce her. She is a heavenly angel incarnate ... who has flown down among us mortals,... if you can understand.”
“Look at him, shaking all over, as though he were in convulsions!” Varvara went on indignantly.

“And she there, stamping her foot at me and calling me a fool a minute ago, she too is a heavenly angel incarnate, and she has good reason to call me one. Come along, Alexey Fyodorovitch, we have to put an end to this.”
And, seizing Alyosha’s hand, he led him out of the room and into the street.
